Date:
OCT
Annie Taylor rides over Niagara Falls
What clue would you check first on October 24?
Have you ever wondered why a small calendar box can open a much bigger
story? On October 24, Teacher Annie Edson Taylor survived going over
Niagara Falls in a barrel on October 24, 1901, attempting a daring
challenge. The research record places this event in 1901, so the class
can compare that year with a nearby starting year of 1890. The title
card says “Annie Taylor rides over Niagara Falls,” and it invites
readers to look for the problem, invention, creature, or challenge
behind the headline. A history detective does not need to memorize every
detail; the detective notices which clues can be checked and which
numbers can be used carefully. In this classroom version, the event-year
clue ends in 1; for the worksheet, each museum panel gets 3 labels, and
the display repeats that set across 2 panels. The passage also names 1
clues that can be set aside after the first round. The timeline
comparison uses 1890 and a gap of 11 years, while the October label 24
helps us connect the math back to the story. The source is Niagara Falls
National Heritage Area, so the event claim is not invented for the
worksheet. After reading, ask what you would check first, whether the
display tells the same story, and how a number can describe a real event
without becoming the whole event. History becomes easier to remember
when a reader asks a question, checks a source, and then explains the
clue in their own words.
